answers.name: the reading list
answers.unclear: Each row is one document, and the order and glosses are edited over time, so registry plus list. The poster's registry reads 'one entry per thing', which suggests full coverage. This is five hand-picked documents, so the 'list' add carries most of the meaning, and the poster does not say whether a hand-chosen subset is still a registry.

answers.name: tracker registry, a cache
answers.unclear: Each entry is one tracker, kept current, and regenerated by tools/generate-tracker-registry.py from the tasks/ folders, so registry plus cache. Entries show counts by status but carry no status of their own, so 'tracker' does not apply. The overlap of the add word 'tracker' with the subject (trackers) is confusing, but the rule is clear.

answers.name: outpost observation stream
answers.unclear: Rows are appended and never rewritten, and dates must not go backwards, so stream. But each row is also a dated reading of one file's state ('verified', 'differs'), which matches snapshot's 'a reading, kept as of its date'. The poster gives no test for telling an observation event from a reading of a thing. I chose stream because the collection grows row by row as observations happen, and an 'installed' row records an act.

answers.collection: window.__traffic, the traffic ledger in lib/gh-boot.js
answers.name: live request window (traffic ledger)
answers.unclear: Each entry is one fetch (an event). It is pushed at send, then rewritten while the request is in flight: status, ms, wire and rate are filled in at settle, and __noteApiError adds msg. That is 'a record rewritten until its event ends'. Past a cap of 400 the oldest rows are spliced off, which is the poster's open call 4 (window). The poster lists 'the traffic logs' as a stream example, which pulls the other way. Those logs are the persisted files under web-tools-private/logs/traffic/, not this in-memory array, but the poster does not tell the two apart.

answers.name: sessions cache
answers.unclear: Each row summarizes one session (an event). The live session's row is re-summarized whenever its record's blob sha moves, which is what the poster puts in the empty box, so no word yet plus cache. It also keeps only the newest 400 rows (ROW_CAP), which is call 4 (window) again. The poster's own example for the empty box is the session records themselves, and it does not say whether a cache over them takes their box or the box of its rows.

answers.name: source snapshots (dated intake bundles)
answers.unclear: A one-intake bundle is a dated folder that is never revised, which is a snapshot. A series bundle is one publisher's product, and it gains new dated intakes over time ('acquired' moves to the latest one), so it changes after it is written, like a registry entry. The poster assigns a box per collection and has no rule for a thing that holds dated snapshots inside it. The bundle and file tables the script writes would be caches, but they are not the bundles.

answers.name: enacted decision stream, a cache
answers.unclear: Each row is one enacted decision (item x session x phase), a fact that does not change once enacted, so stream. The table is a generated mart rebuilt from a dated 2026-06-04 pull plus the driver taxonomy, so cache. But it is rebuilt whole rather than appended 'as things happen', and its classification tags (driver, persistence) change when the taxonomy is revised. The poster does not say whether a derived table built from one dated pull is a stream, or a cache of a snapshot.

answers.name: request queue
answers.unclear: Poster call 3 names errands directly: request files are closed by adding a result file, never change, and are 'not snapshots'. It leaves the word open and recommends 'request queue', so no box fits yet. 'tracker' fits only loosely: an errand is open or closed by whether a result file exists, not by a status field in the entry. A competing reading is 'no word yet': the errand as a whole stays open until a result closes it, and a Gemini ping's result file is rewritten with later replies until it is marked settled, which is 'a record rewritten until its event ends'.

poster: The two questions (is an entry a thing or an event, and does it change after it is written) settled most cases quickly, and the four add words were easy to apply because each states a test you can check against the code (rebuilt from other files, carries a status, leaves once filed, chosen by hand). The 'four calls' section was the most useful part for the hard cases, because it named errands and capped collections outright instead of letting me force them into a box. The poster failed in three places. First, it has no rule for an entry that is a dated reading of a thing, which made observations.csv a coin flip between snapshot and stream. Second, it does not say whether a derived collection (sessions.json, decision-ledger.csv) takes the box of the records it is built from or of its own rows, and 'cache' only answers half of that. Third, its examples are names rather than paths. 'The traffic logs' sits under stream, while the in-memory traffic ledger behaves like the empty box and like a window, and I had to open web-tools-private/logs/traffic/ to work out that these are two different collections. A box assigned per collection also strains when one collection mixes entry kinds, as source bundles do with single intakes and series.
